articles.title: Higher education curricula must adapt to the needs of today’s students
articles.summary: Some programs attract so few majors that they need to be eliminated, and those teaching in them should be absorbed into other departments where possible.
articles.body:
Another academic year is under way, and the crisis in higher education continues as costs remain high and colleges and universities compete for fewer and fewer students.

The decline in enrollments stems in large measure from a decreasing number of traditional college-age people in the general population — what recruiters call the “ enrollment cliff .” In addition, fewer foreign students , a major source of revenue, are choosing to study in the U.S.

Perhaps most importantly, young people are questioning the value of a college education. Those who do opt to pursue a degree have become more discerning in their choice of programs, opting for majors that launch them on a career path. That explains why two-year community colleges , which focus on vocational education and training, are thriving, while tuition-driven four-year institutions struggle.

Colleges and universities cannot do anything about demographic change, nor should they become technical schools. But they can and must restructure their curriculum to align with student demand and the labor market.

The last decades of the 20th century saw the creation of numerous interdisciplinary programs that began as cooperative ventures between established disciplines and evolved into stand-alone departments with all the attendant costs of maintaining them. Interdisciplinary offerings range from vibrant programs geared to the job market, such as those devoted to “environmental policy” and “health information integration” to purely academic ones such as “ cultural, ethnic and gender studies ,” which experienced more than a 20 percent decline in enrollment between 2017 and 2025.

Traditional majors , especially in the humanities, have also lost students. Religion, English and “languages and literature” have been hit hardest.

These trends highlight the need for all institutions of higher learning to undertake a rigorous cost-benefit analysis of all academic programs and majors to determine their long-term viability. Some departments need to be combined, which in some cases should not be difficult. Religion and Philosophy could peacefully coexist as could English and rhetoric. Programs like American studies could survive as concentrations in departments of history or political science.

However, some programs attract so few majors that they need to be eliminated, and those teaching in them should be absorbed into other departments where possible.

Faculty should be at the forefront of curriculum redesign and restructuring, but sadly, too many professors prefer to defend the academic turf they have spent much of their career building. They defend dying majors and programs on their alleged intrinsic worth regardless of enrollment and offer courses based on what they like to teach rather than on what students want or need.

As a result, administrators have stepped in to force restructuring.

Following an extensive portfolio review, Syracuse University is dropping 93 majors, and halting enrollment in several others. Not out of financial necessity, but as “an important step in developing a portfolio that is more focused, more distinctive and more aligned with student demand,” according to Provost Lois Agnew. Loyola University in Chicago is undertaking a similar review to deal with budget cuts and declines in enrollment. The university may eliminate as many as 71 academic programs.

A number of other colleges and universities have made similar cuts in the past few years, including St. Cloud State University in Minnesota, which axed “42 degree programs and 50 minors,” and West Virginia University , which dropped 28 majors and eliminated 143 faculty positions to help cover a $45 million budget shortfall.

These examples cannot be dismissed as isolated incidents. In the next few years, most colleges and universities will have to trim their sails to the prevailing economic and demographic winds in order to better serve their students and even keep their doors open.

Painful though this process may be, the alternative looks far worse. From March 2020 through April, 49 colleges closed and 40 merged .

Since curriculum reform and program restructuring are inevitable, faculty face a clear choice. They can take charge of the process to ensure the best possible outcome for themselves and their students, or they can have change forced upon them by trustees and administrators.

Tom Mockaitis is a professor of history at DePaul University and the author of “ Violent Extremists: Understanding the Domestic and International Terrorist Threat .”

articles.title: Potential Michigan serial killer may have left behind valuable evidence, former FBI profiler says
articles.summary: Former FBI profiler Mary Ellen O'Toole said on "The Big Weekend Show" that the suspected Michigan serial killer likely left valuable forensic evidence in Lansing.
articles.body: A former FBI profiler warns that a potential serial killer in Michigan may have left behind valuable forensic evidence at outdoor crime scenes as authorities investigate whether five deaths in Lansing are connected. Mary Ellen O'Toole told the "The Big Weekend Show" on Saturday that the killings posed risks for the offender because they occurred outdoors where the victims, all believed to have been homeless, were likely sleeping. 'UNMASKING A MONSTER': GOLDEN STATE KILLER SERIES CHALLENGES TIMELINE OF JOSEPH DEANGELO'S CRIMES "It's also very high risk for the offender because the offender comes in to an open area and kills these people — and these are probably not quick homicides — and then has to leave the area." "And I can almost tell you for sure that this offender is not cleaning up his crime scenes," she added. "So he's probably leaving behind some very valuable evidence for investigators to analyze." FOX HOLLOW CORONER REVEALS WHY HE DOUBTS SUSPECTED SERIAL KILLER ACTED ALONE IN HUNT FOR ANSWERS The five victims were discovered near the Lansing River Trail near Michigan State University. The deaths occurred between October 2025 and September 2026. Police arrested a suspect in connection with the stabbing death of one man, but have not linked him to the other deaths. O'Toole said police have more work to do before determining whether the cases are related. That includes examining unsolved homicides in the surrounding area and potentially other states for evidence of earlier crimes by the same offender.
